title: Interfaces, Intersections, and Which to Use
summary: Declare object shapes with interface and extends, combine types with intersections, and choose between interface and type.
intro: `type` aliases are one way to name an object shape. Interfaces are the other, and real codebases use both, often in the same file. In this lesson you declare shapes with `interface` and `extends`, combine them with `&`, see how interface declarations merge, and learn the convention many teams follow for choosing between the two.

steps.title: Interfaces and extends

examples.title: Animals
examples.prompt: Extend an Animal interface into a Dog, and pass a Dog where an Animal is expected.
examples.output:
Hello, Rex!
Rex is a Beagle
examples.explanation: `Dog` has everything `Animal` has plus `breed`, so `rex` needs both properties. Because a `Dog` has every member of `Animal`, it can go to `greet`, which only knows about `name`. This is the same shape check as with type aliases: `extends` just saves you from writing `name: string` again.

examples.title: Several bases
examples.prompt: Build an Admin from a User and an Auditable interface at once.
examples.output:
root@example.com (#1)
created 2026-01-15 by setup
can manage: users, billing
examples.explanation: `extends User, Auditable` copies the members of both interfaces into `Admin`, which then adds `permissions`. Leaving out any of the five properties is a type error that names the missing one. A small interface like `Auditable` can be mixed into many shapes, so the audit fields are written once.

examples.title: Readonly and optional members
examples.prompt: Mark a member's id readonly and its nickname optional, and print a default when the nickname is missing.
examples.explanation: The modifiers work exactly as in type aliases: `id` cannot be reassigned, and `nickname` may be left out, so reading it gives `string | undefined`. `??` falls back to the full name when there is no nickname. With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` on, Alan's object leaves the key out instead of setting it to `undefined`.

practice.title: Employee directory
practice.prompt:
Model a company directory where every employee is also a person.

1. Make `Employee` extend `Person`, adding `team` (a string) and an optional `managerEmail` (a string).
2. Make `directoryLine` return a line like `Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com>, Platform, manager: grace@example.com`, with `none` when there is no manager.

Expected output:

```text
Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com>, Platform, manager: grace@example.com
Grace Hopper <grace@example.com>, Platform, manager: none
Alan Turing <alan@example.com>, Research, manager: grace@example.com
```

tests.output:
Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com>, Platform, manager: grace@example.com
Grace Hopper <grace@example.com>, Platform, manager: none
Alan Turing <alan@example.com>, Research, manager: grace@example.com

cases.name: rejects an employee without a team
cases.code: const e: Employee = { name: "Ada Lovelace", email: "ada@example.com" };

hints: Start with `export interface Employee extends Person`, the way `Dog` extends `Animal` in the first example.
An optional member has a `?` after its name: `managerEmail?: string`.
`employee.managerEmail ?? "none"` gives the manager's email, or `none` when it is missing.

steps.title: Intersections

examples.title: Timestamped posts
examples.prompt: Mix shared timestamp fields into a post with an intersection.
examples.output:
Hello, TypeScript by Ada
created 2026-09-01, updated 2026-09-14
examples.explanation: `Post` is the inline object type and `Timestamped` together, so `post` must have all four properties, and leaving out `updatedAt` would be a type error. Any other shape can reuse `Timestamped` the same way, for example `type Comment = { text: string } & Timestamped`.

examples.title: From new to saved
examples.prompt: Describe the data a user sends for a new task, then the saved task as that data plus an id and a done flag.
examples.explanation: `NewTask` is what a form or a request sends, and `Task` is the same data after saving, plus the fields the program adds. Because `Task` is written as `NewTask & { ... }`, a field added to `NewTask` later shows up in `Task` too. In `save`, `{ ...input, id, done: false }` copies the input's fields and adds the other two, and the return type `Task` checks that nothing is missing.

examples.title: Conflicting members
examples.prompt: Give id two different types, once with an intersection and once with extends.
examples.output:
main.ts(5,24): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'never'.
main.ts(11,11): error TS2430: Interface 'Child' incorrectly extends interface 'Base'.
  Types of property 'id' are incompatible.
    Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.
examples.explanation: In `Both`, `id` must be a `string` and a `number` at once. No value is both, so `id` has the type `never`, and the error only appears on line 5, where a value is created, away from the types that caused it. The interface version fails at the declaration of `Child` instead, and TS2430 says which property conflicts. That earlier, clearer error is one reason to prefer `extends` when you build one object shape from another.

practice.title: Audit fields
practice.prompt:
Add audit fields to invoices with an intersection.

1. Complete `Auditable` with `createdBy` and `updatedBy`, both strings.
2. Make `Invoice` the intersection of `{ number: string; totalCents: number }` and `Auditable`.
3. Make `invoiceLine` return a line like `INV-001: $120.00 (created by ada, updated by grace)`.

Expected output:

```text
INV-001: $120.00 (created by ada, updated by grace)
INV-002: $45.50 (created by alan, updated by alan)
```

tests.output:
INV-001: $120.00 (created by ada, updated by grace)
INV-002: $45.50 (created by alan, updated by alan)

cases.name: rejects an invoice without updatedBy
cases.code: const bad: Invoice = { number: "INV-009", totalCents: 100, createdBy: "ada" };

hints: `Auditable` lists its two properties like any object type.
Put `&` between the inline object type and `Auditable`, the way `Post` adds `Timestamped` in the first example.
Format the total with `(invoice.totalCents / 100).toFixed(2)`, and write a literal `$` before it.

steps.title: Declaration merging and which to use

examples.title: Merging
examples.prompt: Declare Settings in two blocks, then build one object that needs the members of both.
examples.output:
dark theme, language en
14px, word wrap on
examples.explanation: The two declarations merge into one `Settings` with four members, so the object needs all four, and leaving out `fontSize` is a type error. In one file this looks odd, but it is what happens when a library declares an interface and your code, or another package, adds to it. A type alias can never grow like this, which is why some teams prefer aliases for their own shapes.

examples.title: Aliases do not merge
examples.prompt: Declare the same type alias twice.
examples.output:
main.ts(1,6): error TS2300: Duplicate identifier 'Settings'.
main.ts(5,6): error TS2300: Duplicate identifier 'Settings'.
main.ts(9,45): error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'fontSize' does not exist in type 'Settings'.
examples.explanation: A type alias is one name for one type, so declaring `Settings` twice is TS2300, reported at both declarations. The checker then goes on with the first `Settings` only, which is why `fontSize` in the object is also reported, as an excess property (TS2353). To combine two shapes, give each its own name and intersect them: `type Settings = ThemeSettings & EditorSettings`.

examples.title: The convention
examples.prompt: Use a type alias for the status union, and interfaces for the orders that hold it.
examples.explanation: `OrderStatus` is a union, so it has to be a type alias: there is no `interface` form of `"pending" | "paid"`. `Order` and `PaidOrder` are object shapes, so they are interfaces. `PaidOrder` narrows `status` to the single literal `"paid"`, which is allowed because `"paid"` fits `OrderStatus`, so `receipt` only accepts paid orders. A `PaidOrder` is still an `Order`, which is why `summary(done)` compiles.

practice.title: Order model
practice.prompt:
Model orders with a status union, an interface, and an interface for shipped orders that extends it.

1. Make `OrderStatus` a union of `"pending"`, `"paid"`, and `"shipped"`.
2. Give `Order` an `id` (a string), a `status` (an `OrderStatus`), and a `totalCents` (a number).
3. Make `ShippedOrder` extend `Order`, with `status` narrowed to `"shipped"` and a `trackingNumber` (a string).
4. Make `describe` return a line like `B-7 is pending ($18.00)`, and `trackingLabel` a line like `B-9 ships with 1Z999AA1`.

Expected output:

```text
B-7 is pending ($18.00)
B-8 is paid ($42.50)
B-9 ships with 1Z999AA1
```

tests.output:
B-7 is pending ($18.00)
B-8 is paid ($42.50)
B-9 ships with 1Z999AA1

typeTests.imports: import { type Order, type ShippedOrder } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: rejects an order with an unknown status
cases.code: const lost: Order = { id: "X-1", status: "lost", totalCents: 100 };

cases.name: rejects a shipped order whose status is paid
cases.code: const early: ShippedOrder = { id: "X-2", status: "paid", totalCents: 100, trackingNumber: "1Z" };

hints: `OrderStatus` is a union of three string literals joined with `|`, so it stays a `type`.
`interface ShippedOrder extends Order` adds `trackingNumber` and redeclares `status: "shipped"`, the way `PaidOrder` narrows it to `"paid"` in the last example.
`describe` formats the total like the example's `summary`: `(order.totalCents / 100).toFixed(2)` after a literal `$`.

recap:
- `interface Name { ... }` declares an object shape. For object shapes, interfaces and type aliases are interchangeable.
- `interface B extends A` has every member of `A` plus its own, and an interface can extend several at once: `extends A, C`.
- `A & B` intersects two types: a value needs every member of both.
- Conflicting members turn an intersection's property into `never`, while `extends` reports the conflict at the declaration (TS2430).
- Two `interface` declarations with one name merge. Two `type` aliases with one name are an error (TS2300).
- Unions, tuples, function types, and computed types can only be aliases. A common convention: `interface` for object shapes, `type` for the rest.
